content: 1. The manufacturer's instructions should be followed for specific recommendations regarding specimen collection. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are generally not suitable for testing large numbers of blood samples. 2. Laboratory-based immunoassays, such as enzyme immunoassays (EIAs), chemiluminescent immunoassays (CLIAs), and electrochemiluminescent immunoassays (ECLs), are designed to detect antibodies, antigens, or both. These assays differ primarily in their methods of detecting immune complexes. A cut-off value, typically determined by the assay manufacturer, defines the threshold at which results are considered reactive. EIA results are often reported as optical density divided by the assay cut-off (OD/CO) values. 3. These laboratory-based assays are most cost-effective and efficient in settings with high specimen throughput, typically exceeding 40 samples per day. They are intended for use in laboratories or facilities with reliable infrastructure, such as electricity, cold storage, and climate-controlled environments, as well as skilled staff. These assays often require cold-chain storage for test kits and the use of precision pipettes. They are generally performed on serum or plasma specimens, necessitating phlebotomy for proper specimen collection. 4. Laboratory-based immunoassays can be conducted manually or using automated systems, which may be either non-dedicated or specific to the assay. Automated immunoanalysers streamline many processes, reducing the hands-on time required compared to manual EIAs. These systems can be used in a variety of settings, from high-throughput laboratories with full automation to medium-sized laboratories with semi-automation, and even small laboratories in remote areas where tests are conducted manually. 5. Confirmatory assays are used to validate initial test results. For hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), neutralization assays confirm whether observed antigen reactivity can be neutralized by repeating the test with the same specimen and a specific anti-HBs-containing reagent. A confirmed result is achieved when the neutralization reagent eliminates reactivity compared to a control reaction. 6. For anti-HCV (hepatitis C virus antibodies), line immunoassays or immunoblots are used to confirm the presence of antibodies detected by other serological assays. While confirmatory assays provide definitive results, they are more expensive and prone to higher rates of indeterminate results. These assays confirm serostatus but cannot diagnose active HCV infection with viremia. 7. Nucleic acid testing (NAT) technologies detect viral nucleic acids (DNA or RNA) by targeting and amplifying specific viral segments. Amplification allows for the detection of low viral levels that might otherwise be undetectable. Laboratory-based NAT requires sophisticated equipment, stringent laboratory conditions, precise specimen collection, and highly trained staff to avoid contamination and ensure accuracy. 8. Not all NAT technologies detect all viral genotypes or subtypes equally unless optimized for this purpose. Newer NAT technologies are simpler and more robust, designed for use at or near the point of care, potentially overcoming logistical and technical challenges associated with laboratory-based NAT. 9. Multiplex NAT assays have been developed to simultaneously detect DNA or RNA from multiple viruses, in addition to single-virus NAT assays. 10. The choice of assay format depends on factors such as performance characteristics (sensitivity and specificity), cost, ease of use, and the testing site's infrastructure, storage facilities, and staff expertise. WHO recommends standardized testing strategies to maximize accuracy while simplifying processes through streamlined procurement and training. 11. A one-assay serological testing strategy involves performing a single serological test. If the result is reactive, the status is reported as compatible with positive infection. If non-reactive, the status is reported as negative infection. This strategy efficiently rules out most uninfected individuals and identifies those likely to be infected, requiring further testing for viremia and liver disease staging. 12. A two-assay serological testing strategy involves sequentially using two different assays to improve the positive predictive value (PPV) and reduce inappropriate referrals to specialist services. This can involve repeating the test with a different assay of similar sensitivity or performing a neutralization test for HBsAg using a specific anti-HBs reagent. 13. If the first test result is non-reactive, the status is reported as negative infection. If both tests are reactive, the status is reported as presumptive positive infection for further diagnostic testing. If the second test is non-reactive, the status is reported as infection inconclusive; requires additional testing. Using a less sensitive second assay may result in some true positives being missed. 14. WHO recommends routine HBsAg serological testing for all adults in settings with an HBsAg seroprevalence of ≥2% or ≥5%, with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services. Testing should utilize existing communityor facility-based opportunities, such as antenatal clinics or HIV/TB clinics. 15. Routine HBsAg testing is recommended for all pregnant women in settings with an HBsAg seroprevalence of ≥2% or ≥5%, with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services. Partners and family members of those with HBV infection should also be offered testing. 16. Focused testing is recommended for populations most affected by HBV or HCV, such as people with clinical signs of liver disease, sexual partners and household contacts of infected individuals, healthcare workers, and blood donors. Testing should be linked to vaccination for those who are HBsAg-negative and unvaccinated. 17. For HCV, focused testing is recommended for high-risk populations, such as people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, and individuals with HIV. Periodic re-testing using HCV NAT should be considered for those at ongoing risk of infection or reinfection. 18. General population testing for HCV is recommended in settings with an HCV antibody seroprevalence of ≥2% or ≥5%, with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services. Testing should leverage existing communityor facility-based opportunities, such as HIV or TB clinics and drug treatment services. 19. Birth cohort testing may be applied to older individuals at higher risk of HCV infection and morbidity due to historical exposure to unscreened or inadequately screened blood products or unsafe injection practices. 20. Viral hepatitis testing can be delivered through general population testing or focused testing in high-risk populations, using either facility-based or community-based approaches. WHO provides detailed guidance on setting up laboratory services, selecting assays, and ensuring testing quality.
